@graph.headline: What Every Metro Detroit Business Should Know Before Putting Customer Data Into AI
@graph.description: Shadow AI is quietly exposing customer data across Metro Detroit businesses. HIPAA, attorney-client privilege, and trade secrets are all at risk. Here's the compliance checklist — and why a local LLM device may be the safest answer.

about.name: AI Data Privacy and Compliance for Businesses

mainEntity.name: What is shadow AI and why is it risky?

acceptedAnswer.text: Shadow AI is the use of AI tools by employees without company approval or awareness. It's risky because sensitive data — customer information, PHI, privileged communications, trade secrets — can be sent to third-party tools that may train on it, creating compliance violations and data exposure the business never authorized.

mainEntity.name: What data should never be entered into AI tools?

acceptedAnswer.text: Social Security numbers and personal identifiers, protected health information (PHI) covered by HIPAA, attorney-client privileged communications, and proprietary business information such as pricing, processes, and trade secrets.

mainEntity.name: Can a business use AI with patient data and stay HIPAA compliant?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes — but only with HIPAA-compliant AI that includes a signed Business Associate Agreement (BAA), encryption at rest and in transit, and documented breach notification procedures. The safest option is on-premises AI where patient data never leaves the business.

mainEntity.name: How does using public AI tools risk attorney-client privilege?

acceptedAnswer.text: Sharing client information or case details with a third-party AI tool can waive attorney-client privilege, because the client's expectation of confidentiality is compromised the moment the data is disclosed to an outside provider without adequate protections.

mainEntity.name: What is a local LLM device?

acceptedAnswer.text: A local LLM device is a self-contained AI system that runs on hardware you own, on your premises. Models execute locally and your data never leaves the building — eliminating the third-party exposure, training-data, and BAA dependency of cloud AI.

mainEntity.name: Does on-premises AI require a Business Associate Agreement?

acceptedAnswer.text: In most cases, no. A BAA is required when a vendor handles PHI on your behalf. When your own AI runs entirely on your own hardware with no vendor processing your data, the BAA requirement drops away — which is precisely why local LLM devices simplify compliance.
